title: Conversion Functionality Lab
short: Why the form only looks like it works
summary: A landing page whose form shows 'Thanks!' without an email address and whose main button goes somewhere its label does not promise. Find both faults, read the check that catches them fail, and then pass.

guide.title: How to audit a landing page with Claude Code

product.label: Claude Code Conversion & Revenue Optimization Toolkit
product.note: The functional checks in the toolkit are the runnable version of the four questions in this lab, for every landing page you own.

module.title: Generate a functional-validation checklist for your own page

scenario: Harbourline Physio runs an ad campaign to a landing page: 'Book a free 15-minute assessment'. Ad clicks are up; bookings are not. The owner says the page 'works — I filled it in myself'. You have the page's form markup, its validation script, and the output of a browser test someone wrote last month and never ran.

sample.label: Declared sample data
sample.note: The page, the script and the test output are fixtures written for this lab. The landing page is included in the fixture bundle so you can open it locally and run the test yourself; it posts to nothing.

starting: The form markup and script as served. One validation state is broken in a way a person filling in the form correctly will never see. The primary button is a second, separate fault.

steps.title: Which validation state is broken?
steps.instruction: Read the markup and the script together. Ask: what happens when the email field is empty?

decision.question: What does the page do with an empty email?

options.label: It shows 'Thanks!' and posts the form. The email input has no required attribute and type="text", the form is novalidate, and the script checks only the name — so a visitor who skips the one field the clinic needs is told it worked.
The browser blocks it: the input is required.
The server rejects it, and the page shows the server's error.
Nothing is broken; the owner filled it in and it worked.

explain.correct: Three things combine: no required on the email field, novalidate on the form (so the browser would not check even type="email"), and a script that returns early only for a blank name. The success message is written unconditionally after fetch() is called — not after it succeeds. Anyone who fills the form in fully never sees this; that is why 'I tried it myself' proves nothing about the states you did not try.

wrong.browser: Look at the email input: no required attribute, type="text", and the form has novalidate. The browser has been told to stay out of it.
wrong.server: The script does not await the response or read it; it writes 'Thanks!' regardless. Whatever the server says, the visitor sees success.
wrong.fine: The owner tested the happy path. The broken state is the one where the email is missing — the one a rushed visitor on a phone hits.

steps.title: Where does the button go?
steps.instruction: The label promises a booking. Read the href.

decision.question: What is wrong with the primary call to action?

options.label: It links to /contact — a generic contact page — while its label promises the booking form. The visitor who clicks the promise lands on something else and has to find the form again.

explain.correct: Message match is not only ad-to-page; it is label-to-destination. A button that says 'Book' and lands on 'Contact us' breaks the promise at the moment of highest intent. The third test in the run asserts exactly this and fails with the received URL.

wrong.nothing: The contact page is not the assessment form; it does not ask for a preferred time, and it does not say 'free 15-minute assessment'. Every step between the click and the promised thing loses people.
wrong.text: Length is a design preference. The destination is a functional fault the test can prove.

steps.title: Read the failing run
steps.instruction: Someone wrote the test last month and never ran it. Read the two failures.

decision.question: What do the two failures prove?

options.label: Test 2 proves the empty-email state shows the success message (received 'Thanks!', expected a message about email). Test 3 proves the CTA lands on /contact. Both faults are reproduced by a check, not an opinion.
The tests are flaky; they should be rerun.
That bookings are not being emailed to reception.

explain.correct: The value of a test that fails is that it names the received value. 'Received: Thanks! We will email you to confirm.' is the whole diagnosis of test 2 in one line. Note the test does not prove anything about email delivery — the fixture posts to nothing and the suite mocks nothing about the inbox.

wrong.flaky: Both failures print a deterministic received value that matches the markup you just read. Rerunning a test whose failure you can explain is a way of not fixing it.
wrong.delivery: No test here touches an inbox. A browser test can prove the page posted; it cannot prove anyone received anything. Delivery is checked by a marked submission and a look at the inbox, which is the contact-form Weekly Fix.

steps.title: After the fix: what does green prove?
steps.instruction: The email field gained required and type="email", the script checks it, the success message now waits for a 2xx response, and the CTA points at #book. Read the second run.

decision.question: What does the passing run establish?

options.label: That the two states the tests cover now behave as specified — the empty email is rejected before any success message, and the CTA lands on the form. Nothing about delivery, and nothing about states the suite does not cover.

explain.correct: Green is exactly as wide as the assertions. This suite covers three states; a fourth (a malformed email such as 'bob@') would need a fourth test. And the mocked route in the passing run means the page's request was intercepted — the real endpoint was never called, by design, because this ran on a laptop, not production.

wrong.works: 'Works' is not a test. Three states were asserted; those three are known. The suite says nothing about the ones it does not cover.
wrong.conversion: No test measures behaviour of people. It removed two reasons bookings were lost; whether they rise is observed in the booking count over the following weeks.

after.title: npx playwright test — after the fix
after.content:
Running 3 tests using 1 worker

  ✓  1 assessment.spec.ts:6  › required name shows an error (398ms)
  ✓  2 assessment.spec.ts:14 › empty email is rejected before a success message (455ms)
     (route /api/book mocked: fulfilled 200 {"ok":true} — no real request left the page)
  ✓  3 assessment.spec.ts:27 › primary CTA lands on the booking form (301ms)

  3 passed (2.1s)

closing: Two faults a person testing the happy path never sees, both reproduced by a check that prints what it received. The Playwright guide builds this suite from scratch, including the mocked submission, and the contact-form Weekly Fix covers the part no browser test can: whether the message arrived.
